But his legs would not lift him. He could wait here, and someone might find him. Or he could return home. But his friend would lose his life instead. For one awful moment, that felt easier than standing up.

specs.speaker: narrator

specs.speaker: narrator

specs.speaker: narrator

specs.speaker: narrator
specs.text: You think I am mad, but I am only nervous. Illness made my senses stronger, especially my hearing. I hear everything in heaven and on earth. Listen, and judge how calmly I tell you this. I loved the old man who lived with me. He never hurt me, and I wanted none of his money. But a cloudy film covered his pale blue eye. That vulture's eye made my blood turn cold. I had to get free of it.

specs.speaker: narrator
specs.text: At midnight for seven nights, I slowly opened his door. You should have seen my patience—he never even moved! Then I let one thin ray escape from my lantern. But I always found that eye shut. I could not act: I hated his eye, not him. Every morning, I kindly asked about his night's sleep. On night eight, I almost laughed at my own cleverness. Then my thumb slipped on the catch of my lantern.

specs.speaker: old_man
specs.text: "Who is in here?"

specs.speaker: narrator
specs.text: he shouted.

specs.speaker: narrator
specs.text: For an hour, he sat listening while I stood completely still. Finally, he groaned softly in fear, not pain. I knew that sound well. I opened the lantern's cover, sending light onto his eye. It was completely open now. I heard low, quick beats, like a watch wrapped in cotton. His heart grew faster and louder—what if a neighbour heard? I rushed at him, and he gave one scream. I pulled him down and covered him with the heavy bed. Finally his heart stopped, and I could feel no pulse. I hid his body under three floorboards, then replaced them exactly. You could search all night and find no mark. At four that morning, three police officers arrived and knocked. A neighbour had heard a scream from the house.

specs.speaker: narrator
specs.text: I welcomed them and blamed my scream on a bad dream. I said the old man was away in the country. After showing every room, I brought chairs into his bedroom. You see, I sat right above the body without fear. They talked in a friendly way while I smiled. My head started hurting, and I heard a ringing sound. No—it was that low, quick beating once again. I raised my voice, but the beating grew louder too. I walked about and scraped my chair across the floorboards. They went on talking and smiling as before. The sound kept growing louder and louder! Could you bear that? They heard and knew—they were laughing at me! I could not stand any more. "I killed him!" I screamed. "Pull up the floorboards here! That is the beating of his horrible heart!"

chunks.text: I stood motionless. For an hour he sat in bed, listening. At last he groaned softly. Not pain—terror. I knew that sound. I uncovered the lantern. Its narrow beam found the eye. Wide open. A low, quick beating reached me, like a watch wrapped in cotton. His heart! Faster it went, and louder. What if a neighbour heard?

I rushed forward. He shrieked once. I dragged him down and pulled the heavy bed over him. Finally, the beating stopped. I checked his pulse. Nothing. I hid his body beneath three floorboards and fitted them back exactly. Not a mark! You could have searched all night. At four in the morning, three police officers knocked. A neighbour had heard a shriek.

I welcomed them. A bad dream, I explained; the cry was mine. The old man was away in the country. I showed them every room, then brought chairs into his bedroom. I sat directly above the body. You see how little I feared? They chatted pleasantly. I smiled. Then my head began to ache. A ringing filled my ears—but no. That low, quick beating again.

I spoke louder. It grew louder too. I paced and scraped my chair across the boards. Still they chatted. Still they smiled. Louder. Louder! Could you have borne it? They heard! They knew! Their smiles were mocking me. I could bear no more. "I did it!" I screamed. "Tear up the planks! Here! It is the beating of his hideous heart!"
